description.description_long: The dispute began with Spain’s refusal to let U.S. forces use jointly operated bases in southern Spain for attacks connected to the Iran conflict. Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said the government would not permit the bases to support actions outside the United Nations Charter, and Spain said the facilities had not been used in the weekend’s strikes. On March 3, President Donald Trump responded by threatening to end trade with Spain. He also complained that Madrid had not accepted NATO’s proposed five-percent defense-spending target, even though Spain said it was meeting its commitments. Trump asserted that the United States could use the bases if it wanted to, despite Spain’s stated position. The threat raised a separate practical question: Spain does not negotiate trade policy alone, because the European Union handles trade agreements on behalf of its 27 member states. A spokesperson for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said any review would have to respect Spain’s autonomy, international law and EU-U.S. agreements. The European Commission likewise said it expected the United States to honor its trade arrangement with the bloc. Trump’s announcement followed a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that invalidated broad tariffs, and he suggested an embargo could provide another route. The immediate reporting established a threat and a disagreement over military access and NATO spending; it did not establish that trade with Spain was actually halted.

description.description_long: An NPR investigation published February 24, 2026, found that the Justice Department had withheld or removed some Epstein-related records concerning allegations against President Donald Trump. NPR compared serial numbers across the public database, FBI case files, emails and discovery logs from Ghislaine Maxwell’s criminal case, identifying 53 pages of interview documents and notes that appeared to be missing from the public release. The records included material related to a woman who told the FBI that Epstein introduced her to Trump when she was a minor; NPR reported that only one of four interviews with her was publicly available and that the available interview did not mention Trump. The report also described files concerning a second woman whose interview materials were removed and later restored, as well as another related document that remained offline. These were allegations in investigative records, not findings of guilt. The White House said Trump had been exonerated and denied wrongdoing. DOJ declined to explain the specific omissions to NPR, saying more generally that unpublished material could be privileged, duplicative or connected to an ongoing investigation; the department also said some temporary removals allowed additional review for victim privacy. The investigation documented gaps and described how NPR identified them, but it did not establish why each file was unavailable. Its findings renewed questions about the completeness and handling of the public release while the allegations themselves remained unadjudicated.

description.description_long: The Atlantic launched “Unthinkable” in January 2019 as a collection of 50 essays on events from Donald Trump’s first two years in office. The magazine asked writers to describe moments they considered especially significant or difficult to imagine in a more conventional presidency. The project included essays about Trump’s attacks on the press, disputes over intelligence and law enforcement, the longest government shutdown, and the separation of families at the border. Its format was a retrospective selection of episodes rather than a longitudinal study of institutional stamina. The page does not demonstrate that Trump’s rhetoric caused institutions to tire or that resistance became less consistent over time. It also does not measure public trust or compare agencies’ responses across administrations. The source supports the existence and subject matter of the retrospective, but not the title’s causal claim about institutional fatigue. A specific event can be examined through one of its essays, while the project as a whole should be described as an editorial collection of notable moments.

description.description_long: Donald Trump systematically expanded religious exemptions to authorize faith-based organizations receiving federal funding to discriminate against LGBTQ+ individuals, women, and religious minorities in employment, services, and program delivery while maintaining taxpayer support for discriminatory practices. The comprehensive discrimination authorization represented implementation of Project 2025's vision to 'increase support for faith-based institutions to discriminate on the basis of sex based on religious beliefs,' creating hostile environments for students, employees, and service recipients who didn't conform to conservative Christian doctrine. The religious exemption expansion allowed federally funded adoption agencies to refuse working with same-sex couples, disaster relief organizations to deny assistance to LGBTQ+ individuals, healthcare providers to refuse treatment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and educational institutions to exclude students based on religious opposition to their identity or conduct. Project 2025's systematic discrimination included permitting faith-based employers to fire unmarried women who engage in sexual conduct, exclude transgender individuals from services, and deny equal treatment to religious minorities while continuing to receive federal grants, contracts, and tax-exempt status. The authorization violated equal protection principles by using taxpayer funds to support discriminatory practices, while creating two-tiered service delivery systems where access to federally funded programs depended on conformity to specific religious beliefs rather than need or eligibility. The faith-based discrimination expansion represented what civil rights organizations called 'weaponization of religious freedom' that transformed constitutional protections for religious practice into licenses for systematic discrimination against vulnerable populations using federal resources.

description.description_long: Donald Trump nominated Erica Schwartz to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in April 2026. The Guardian identified Schwartz as a rear admiral in the U.S. Coast Guard and a former deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first administration. The nomination placed an experienced public-health official in consideration for a major federal health role, but the announcement alone did not change CDC policy or put Schwartz in office. Her appointment depended on the confirmation process. Reporting in July described other health nominees as still awaiting votes, placing the CDC choice amid broader questions about staffing and leadership across federal health agencies. The reports do not give a complete vacancy count or measure how staffing affected CDC operations. The event is a personnel decision: who Trump selected to lead the agency and when the administration put that name forward. It leaves separate the broader criticism of health-agency staffing from the documented facts of Schwartz’s background and nomination.

description.description_long: In 2016, four former contestants from the 1997 Miss Teen USA pageant told reporters that Donald Trump entered their dressing room while contestants were changing. The accounts were not uniform: some other contestants said they did not recall him entering, and some disputed aspects of the allegations. Trump’s campaign denied the claims. PolitiFact’s review also separated the allegations about the teen pageant from Trump’s 2005 Howard Stern interview, in which he described going backstage at his pageants; those remarks referred to adult pageants and did not independently confirm the specific Miss Teen USA accounts. That distinction matters because the claim concerns minors and should be described according to what the contestants reported, rather than treated as an undisputed finding. The episode prompted renewed scrutiny of Trump’s past role in pageants and the power an owner held over contestants. PolitiFact did not issue a definitive rating because some accounts were anonymous and recollections differed. The entry records allegations and a denial, not a legal determination that the conduct occurred.

description.description_long: CNN’s December 2022 report covered the first Trump digital trading-card collection, whose cards depicted him in costumes including a superhero, cowboy and astronaut. The cards were offered for $99 each, and the collection’s website said it was sold out. CNN reported that the collection rose to the top of OpenSea’s rankings and had generated more than $1.4 million since launch, while noting it was unclear how much Trump personally would receive. A disclosure on the site said the collection was licensed to NFT INT LLC and was not owned, managed or controlled by Trump or his companies. The article placed the launch in a declining NFT market: overall trading volume had fallen sharply from its January 2022 peak, and major collections had lost value. This account supports details about the first launch and its timing, not the title’s broader claim about five collections through 2025 or more than $50 million in combined proceeds. Sources documenting each later series, total receipts, buyer outcomes and any access benefits are needed to complete that account.

description.description_long:
Nicaragua received Temporary Protected Status after Hurricane Mitch devastated the country in 1998. On November 6, 2017, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Elaine Duke announced that the designation would be terminated. DHS said conditions related to the hurricane had improved and that Nicaraguan nationals should prepare to return or seek another immigration status. The Federal Register notice gave beneficiaries a 12-month transition and set January 5, 2019, as the planned effective date. At the time, roughly 2,500 Nicaraguans were protected under the designation.

The announced termination did not take effect on that date. In litigation brought by TPS beneficiaries, a federal court issued an injunction that kept the designation and related work authorization in place while the case proceeded. In June 2023, DHS formally rescinded the prior termination and extended the designation. A later administration made a separate termination decision in 2025, with DHS reporting that the designation ended September 8 of that year. These later actions are distinct from Duke’s 2017 announcement: this entry concerns the first Trump administration’s decision and its initially planned end date, not an uninterrupted loss of protection beginning in 2019.
description.description_medium: On November 6, 2017, Acting DHS Secretary Elaine Duke announced that Nicaragua’s Temporary Protected Status designation would end, citing recovery from Hurricane Mitch. The government set a 12-month transition, with termination scheduled for January 5, 2019. A court injunction later blocked implementation, and DHS rescinded the 2017 termination in 2023. A separate 2025 decision subsequently ended the designation effective September 8, 2025.
